sections.name: File setup
sections.title: Shared setup and excluded input folders
sections.what: Sets up the imports and defines the folders for client input data that this fingerprint is meant to leave out. It is the setup for the rest of the file.
sections.why: The comment says client input custody is checked separately, so the fingerprint should not depend on private input files.
sections.watch_out: Changing this list changes every future fingerprint, so older release records will no longer match.

sections.name: workspace_fingerprint (part 1)
sections.title: Fingerprinting the project source files
sections.what: Builds one fingerprint from the source folders and key config files, skipping build output, caches, and generated files. Any change to a counted file changes the result.
sections.why: Likely reason: release evidence needs a deterministic code that proves which source was checked.
sections.watch_out: The exclusion of client input folders compares a three-part path to a three-name list, so it may not exclude those folders as intended.

sections.name: workspace_fingerprint (part 2)
sections.title: Blank separator line
sections.what: Contains no code. It is only the blank line that separates the fingerprint function from the next one.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code.

sections.name: git_identity
sections.title: Recording git commit and cleanliness
sections.what: Asks git for the current commit ID and the list of uncommitted or untracked changes. It returns those with a clean-worktree flag and the source fingerprint.
sections.why: Likely reason: a release record should say which commit was used and whether any unsaved edits were present.
sections.watch_out: Each git call stops with an error if it fails, so the caller must be run inside a git repository.

summary: Creates a repeatable fingerprint of the project's source files and records the git commit state, so release checks can show exactly what was tested.
purpose: Gives the release tools one shared way to say which exact source version was verified.
why: Likely reason: a release record must be tied to one exact set of files. The docstring says the client input exclusion is the explicit scope of a new package feature.
how: The fingerprint walks a fixed list of top-level folders and key config files, skips build output and local client input folders, then hashes each file's relative name and contents in sorted order into one SHA-256 value. Separately, git reports the current commit and whether the working folder has uncommitted or untracked changes.
inputs: The project root folder path. A git repository in that folder, with git installed.
outputs: A hexadecimal fingerprint string from workspace_fingerprint, and a dictionary from git_identity with the commit ID, a clean-worktree flag, the list of changed files, and the fingerprint.
risks: The exclusion check for client input folders compares the first three path parts of each file with the full three-name list. That comparison is unlikely to ever match, so files in those folders may still be fingerprinted, which contradicts the comment. This is not certain from reading alone and should be tested. git_identity stops with an error if git is missing or the folder is not a repository.
debug: If the fingerprint changes unexpectedly, look for new or changed files under the scanned folders, including generated files. If git_identity fails, confirm git is installed and the project root is a git repository. To check the client input exclusion, list the files that workspace_fingerprint includes from the reference folder.
